entity.name: Miguel de Cervantes
entity.description: One-armed soldier who wrote the first modern novel. Cervantes lost the use of his left hand at the Battle of Lepanto, spent five years as a slave in Algiers, was jailed for tax irregularities, and died in poverty — but Don Quixote, published when he was 57, made Spanish itself "the language of Cervantes."

story.name: Miguel de Cervantes
story.description: Wounded at Lepanto, enslaved in Algiers, jailed in Seville, and broke in Madrid — then at 57 publishes the novel that invents modern fiction. A soldier-turned-writer's improbable literary triumph.

moments.name: Miguel de Cervantes Is Born in Alcala de Henares to a Struggling Barber-Surgeon
moments.subtitle: The future author of Don Quixote grows up in a family constantly fleeing creditors
moments.description: Around 29 September 1547, Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra was born in Alcala de Henares, a university town east of Madrid. His father Rodrigo was a barber-surgeon who was frequently in debt and moved the family constantly to avoid creditors. Rodrigo was even imprisoned for debt from October 1553 to April 1554, leaving Cervantes' mother Leonor to support seven children on her own. The family lived in Cordoba, Seville, and finally Madrid, and the young Cervantes likely attended a Jesuit college in Seville. This itinerant, financially precarious childhood would echo throughout Cervantes' life — he spent much of his adult years in poverty, producing the greatest work of Spanish literature while struggling to eat.

moments.name: Cervantes Loses the Use of His Left Hand at the Battle of Lepanto
moments.subtitle: Sick with malaria, commanding a 12-man skiff, the future novelist takes three wounds
moments.description: On 7 October 1571, Miguel de Cervantes fought aboard the galley Marquesa at the Battle of Lepanto, the largest naval engagement in the Mediterranean since antiquity. The Holy League fleet under Don John of Austria defeated the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras, a victory that halted Ottoman expansion into the western Mediterranean. Despite suffering from malaria, Cervantes commanded a 12-man skiff used to assault enemy galleys. He received three wounds — two in the chest and one that permanently disabled his left hand, earning him the lifelong nickname "El manco de Lepanto" (the one-handed man of Lepanto). Cervantes later wrote that he had lost the use of his left hand for the glory of his right.

moments.name: Ottoman Corsairs Capture Cervantes and Hold Him Slave in Algiers for Five Years
moments.subtitle: Four escape attempts fail before a religious charity finally pays his ransom
moments.description: On 26 September 1575, the galley Sol carrying Miguel de Cervantes and his brother Rodrigo was captured by Ottoman corsairs as it approached Barcelona. The brothers were taken to Algiers, where Cervantes was held for ransom. Letters of commendation from Don John of Austria found on Cervantes convinced his captors he was a high-ranking figure, raising the ransom demand beyond what his family could afford. Rodrigo was ransomed in 1577, but Cervantes remained enslaved for nearly five years, attempting four escapes — all of which failed. In 1580, the Trinitarians, a religious charity specializing in ransoming Christian captives, finally secured his freedom. The experience of captivity profoundly shaped his literary imagination.

moments.name: Cervantes Publishes Don Quixote at Age 57, Inventing the Modern Novel
moments.subtitle: A broke, one-armed ex-soldier produces what many call the greatest book ever written
moments.description: In January 1605, the first part of Don Quixote was published in Madrid when Miguel de Cervantes was 57 years old. The story of a delusional hidalgo who mistakes windmills for giants became an immediate bestseller, with pirated editions appearing within weeks. Cervantes had spent decades in poverty — working as a tax collector, briefly jailed for accounting irregularities, and failing to secure a colonial posting in the Americas. Don Quixote is widely considered the first modern novel, blending comedy, tragedy, and metafiction in ways no previous work had attempted. Part Two followed in 1615, partly to reclaim the story from an unauthorized sequel by a pseudonymous author. Spanish is still called "the language of Cervantes."

moments.name: Cervantes Dies in Madrid on the Same Week as Shakespeare
moments.subtitle: Two titans of world literature die days apart in April 1616, though on different calendars
moments.description: On 22 April 1616, Miguel de Cervantes died in Madrid at the age of 68. He was buried the following day, 23 April, which was long mistakenly cited as his death date. William Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616 in England, though because Spain had adopted the Gregorian calendar and England still used the Julian, the two deaths were actually ten days apart. Cervantes had joined the Third Order Franciscans in 1613 and spent his final years in modest circumstances, despite Don Quixote's enormous commercial success. His last novel, The Travails of Persiles and Sigismunda, was published posthumously in 1617. Today, 23 April is celebrated as World Book Day in honor of both authors.
